en.title: Lanterns Just Rewrote Hal Jordan's Worst Comic Moment
en.summary: HBO's Lanterns delivered a stunning blow in episode 5, pushing Hal Jordan and John Stewart to a new low. But for one Lantern, the show's darkest hour isn't the worst of his life.
en.body:
The latest episode of HBO's **Lanterns**, titled "Lights Out," has plunged Hal Jordan and John Stewart into a profound state of conflict, showcasing a level of distrust that feels particularly jarring given their heroic status. As the villainous Antaan confirms Zoe's identity as the Manhunter and launches a devastating attack on Rushville, Hal and John find themselves locked in a bitter feud, their bickering nearly as destructive as the enemy onslaught. This episode marks a significant nadir for their partnership in the series, a disappointing dip in quality for a season that has otherwise been a compelling watch.

However, "Lights Out" doesn't represent the absolute worst moment for either Green Lantern, especially when we consider their extensive comic book histories. John Stewart's own journey has seen darker days, famously marked by his arrogance leading to the catastrophic destruction of the planet Xanshi. Yet, for Hal Jordan, the sting of "Lights Out" pales in comparison to the infamous "Emerald Twilight" storyline. This era in the comics saw Hal's descent into villainy, a dramatic and traumatic period that has long been a sore spot for fans debating his character's portrayal across different media.

## Hal Jordan's Comic Book Low Point

Discussions on any Green Lantern fan forum inevitably touch upon the controversial arcs of Hal Jordan. Even in his early days, as depicted in the beloved **Green Lantern/Green Arrow** series of the 1970s, Hal was often criticized for his rigid adherence to authority, a trait that some fans saw as "bootlicking." He frequently grappled with disillusionment regarding his superhero life, often retreating into periods of personal turmoil. But these personal struggles were dwarfed by the seismic events of "Emerald Twilight," where, driven by grief and madness, Hal destroyed the Green Lantern Corps and became the villainous Parallax. The show's "Lights Out" offers a dramatic conflict, but it's a far cry from Hal's comic-book nadir.

## John Stewart's Controversial Reimagining

Meanwhile, **Lanterns** has also courted significant fan debate with its radical reimagining of John Stewart's origin. Episode 3, "Outkast," presented a stark departure from the comics, focusing heavily on his background, race, and the specific circumstances of his selection as a Green Lantern. This bold narrative choice has polarized viewers, with some praising the show's willingness to explore new thematic territory and others feeling it disrespects the established lore.

> "How the f*** was I not supposed to be scared? Got lifted out of my bed. I was in a…a bubble." — John Sr.

This deviation from the source material, while sparking controversy, has undeniably made for a more engaging and talked-about series. The dynamic between the "old timer" Hal and the "rookie" John, initially lauded as a buddy-comedy setup, has now been tested by these internal and external pressures, making their journey all the more compelling for viewers invested in the nuances of their relationship and their place within the wider DC mythos.

## What's Next

The repercussions of "Lights Out" and the ongoing exploration of John Stewart's altered origin will undoubtedly shape the remainder of **Lanterns**' first season. Fans will be watching closely to see if Hal and John can overcome their animosity and if the show will further explore the darker corners of the Green Lantern universe.

content_raw: This article contains spoilers for Lanterns season 1 episode 5 From episode one, Lanterns has made it clear that Hal Jordan and John Stewart don’t trust each other. But we really thought that when the chips are down and things get bad, these guys would pull it together and figure out how to work with one another. After all, these guys are heroes, right? Yet, when Antaan finally gets confirmation that Zoe is the Manhunter he has been looking for and starts their attack, and as Zoe and her husband Will Macon launch their counter-offensive and tear Rushville apart, Hal and John spend just as much time sniping at each other as they do fighting the bad guys. Episode five, “Lights Out,” is the lowest point for this version of Hal and John, a problem made worse by the fact that the episode is a marked step down in quality for a season that has been great otherwise. But it is not, in fact, the worst point in either character’s life, at least not when you take into account the comics. We talked a bit about John’s worst moment a few weeks back , when his arrogance led to the destruction of the planet Xanshi. But “Lights Out” isn’t the worst moment for Hal Jordan, not while Emerald Twilight still exists. Lights Out for Hal Jordan Go to any comic book forum supporting or decrying the treatment of Hal Jordan in Lanterns , and you’ll quickly find a series of well-documented offenses against Earth’s most famous Green Lantern. Like all GL’s, Hal is a cop, and the beloved Green Lantern/Green Arrow series of the 1970s never missed an opportunity to call out his bootlicking. Throughout that period, and even before, Hal would regularly get bummed out about the whole superheroing thing and would wander around the United States, trying his hand at various jobs such as truck driving, insurance selling, and even toy selling. And, yes, most infamously, he dated Arisia, who was 13 when he met her and then used her ring to give herself an adult body. Yet, Hal Jordan’s blackest night came with the Emerald Twilight storyline from 1994, written by Ron Marz and penciled by Darryl Banks. Emerald Twilight spins out of the Reign of the Superman storyline happening in Superman comics, in which a cyborg who looks like Superman attacks the Earth, destroying Hal’s hometown of Coast City, killing everyone he loves, including on and off romantic interest Carol Ferris and his best friend Tom Kalmaku. As a Green Lantern, Hal has the most powerful weapon in the universe on his finger. And he has more willpower than perhaps any other GL, especially when stricken with grief. So he initially uses his ring to rebuild the city. But when one ring proves insufficient to recreate a major metropolis full of people, Hal entreats the Guardians to either increase his power or send other GLs to help.
